subskill: Range of k keeping a solution count small
prompt:
x ≤ k
kx ≥ -60
In the system of inequalities above, k is a constant. For some integer values of k, the system has at most 19 integer solutions. What is the difference between the greatest and least such values of k?
explanation: If k = 0, the second inequality reads 0 ≥ -60, which is always true, so every integer x ≤ 0 is a solution: infinitely many. If k < 0, dividing kx ≥ -60 by the negative k reverses it: x ≤ 60/(-k). Both inequalities then bound x from above only, so again there are infinitely many solutions. If k > 0, the second inequality gives x ≥ -60/k, so the solutions are the integers from -60/k (rounded up) through k. Their number is k + (the greatest integer not above 60/k) + 1, because when 60/k is an integer the endpoint x = -60/k is included (the sign is ≥). Check the values: k = 4 gives -15 through 4, which is 20; k = 5 gives -12 through 5, which is 18; k = 14 gives -4 through 14 (60/14 = 4.29), which is 19; k = 15 gives -4 through 15, which is 20. Between 5 and 14 the count stays at most 19 (it dips to 16 at k = 7, 8, 9), and outside that range it is larger. So the qualifying k are 5 through 14, and the difference is 14 - 5 = 9. Choice 11 comes from treating kx ≥ -60 as strict: then x = -15 is lost at k = 4 and x = -4 is lost at k = 15, both counts drop to 19, and the range becomes 4 through 15. Choice 12 comes from counting the integers from a to b as b - a instead of b - a + 1, which lowers every count by one and widens the range to 4 through 16. Choice 14 is the greatest qualifying value of k, not the difference.
solve: const cnt=(k)=>{let c=0;for(let x=-6000;x<=6000;x++){if(x<=k&&k*x>=-60)c++;}return c;};const L=[];for(let k=-500;k<=500;k++){if(cnt(k)<=19)L.push(k);}return L[L.length-1]-L[0];

distractor_solve.11: const cnt=(k)=>{let c=0;for(let x=-6000;x<=6000;x++){if(x<=k&&k*x>-60)c++;}return c;};const L=[];for(let k=-500;k<=500;k++){if(cnt(k)<=19)L.push(k);}return L[L.length-1]-L[0];
distractor_solve.12: const cnt=(k)=>{let c=0;for(let x=-6000;x<=6000;x++){if(x<=k&&k*x>=-60)c++;}return c-1;};const L=[];for(let k=-500;k<=500;k++){if(cnt(k)<=19)L.push(k);}return L[L.length-1]-L[0];
distractor_solve.14: const cnt=(k)=>{let c=0;for(let x=-6000;x<=6000;x++){if(x<=k&&k*x>=-60)c++;}return c;};const L=[];for(let k=-500;k<=500;k++){if(cnt(k)<=19)L.push(k);}return L[L.length-1];

mechanism: k ≤ 0 gives an unbounded set (reverse the sign for k < 0)
quantity_asked: the greatest integer k minus the least integer k for which the system has at most 19 integer solutions

setup.i: k is both the upper bound on x and the coefficient of x in the second inequality of a system, so for positive k the solution count k + floor(60/k) + 1 falls and then rises, and k ≤ 0 gives infinitely many
setup.iii: difference between the greatest and least integer values of k

plugback.why: The options are differences between two k values. Trying 9 first, a student cannot substitute 9 as k to confirm a difference (k = 9 qualifies, but that says nothing about the range); confirming 9 needs both boundary values, 5 and 14, and the check that 4 and 15 fail, which is the whole solution.
plugback.aggregate_over: the least and greatest integer k (5 and 14) for which the system has at most 19 integer solutions, with every k ≤ 0 excluded because it gives infinitely many

11.why: Treating ≥ as > drops the attained endpoint -60/k exactly when k divides 60, which lowers the counts at k = 4 and k = 15 to 19, so both ends of the range move outward. A student cannot tell from the stem that losing a solution widens the range.

12.why: Counting the integers from a to b as b - a undercounts every set by one, so more k pass 'at most 19' at both ends. The stem gives no signal that an undercount widens rather than narrows the answer.

14.why: Reporting the greatest qualifying k instead of the difference swaps the asked quantity; whether that lands above or below depends on the sign of the least k, which the stem does not show.

counter_error.solve: const cnt=(k)=>{let c=0;for(let x=-6000;x<=6000;x++){if(x<=k&&k*x>=-60)c++;}return c+1;};const L=[];for(let k=-500;k<=500;k++){if(cnt(k)<=19)L.push(k);}return L[L.length-1]-L[0];
counter_error.why: Counting the integers from a to b as b - a + 2 (an overcount by one) raises every count, so fewer k pass at most 19: the range shrinks to 5 through 13 and the difference to 8, below the key and not an option.

far_distractor.why: Excluding an attained endpoint loses a solution, which ordinarily shrinks an answer; here, with an 'at most' condition on a count that falls and then rises in k, losing a solution lets k = 4 and k = 15 pass, so the range widens and the difference lands above the key.

structure_check: The count falls and then rises in k, and the condition is an upper bound on it. Whether an error widens or narrows the range depends on whether it lowers or raises the counts: undercounting and the strict reading widen it (11, 12, above), overcounting narrows it (counter-error 8, below), and reporting one end swaps the quantity. The stem gives no monotone property that sends every error the same way.
cheap_bound_check: The cheapest bound is that for k > 0 the solutions include 0 through k, so k + 1 ≤ 19 and k ≤ 18; with k ≥ 1 the difference is at most 17. It strikes nothing (all options are at most 14), and 11, 12 and 14 sit on the key's side of it with the key.
intermediate_check: 11: from the range 4 to 15; 9 does not follow from 11 through a printed relation - no. 12: from the range 4 to 16; 12 - 9 = 3 is not printed - no. 14: the greatest k; reaching 9 needs the least k 5, which is not printed - no.
shape_check: The stem hands over that k is an integer, that k must be positive (k ≤ 0 gives infinitely many), and, cheaply, that the difference is at most 17. All four options are positive integers at most 17; no parity is forced, so all four survive together.
interior_parity_check: The two middle values 11 and 12 are both two-digit integers of the same form; neither is cleaner, and the key 9 is an end value.
arith_class_check: Options 9, 11, 12, 14: the key 9 is odd with 11; 9 and 12 are multiples of 3; no divisor of 60 or other class isolates 9.

idea_probe.nearest: e0559aab (system with k in a strict upper bound; the integer solutions sum to -18; sum of k): there k only shifts one bound and the condition is a fixed sum of solutions; here k is both the upper bound and the coefficient of x, so the count k + floor(60/k) + 1 is not monotone in k, k ≤ 0 gives infinitely many, and the ask is the width of the range satisfying an upper bound on the count

dup_search.nearest: e0559aab - k shifts one bound with a sum-of-solutions condition; here k plays two roles and the count falls then rises

self_audit.note: Covering the work, all four options remain legal from the stem alone: the cheapest bound (difference at most 17) strikes none, and no parity or class is forced. Direction: undercounting and the strict reading go above, overcounting goes below (8, the counter-error), so a student cannot tell which way every error goes, and no single bound strikes all three distractors. Try 1 slot: the key 9 is the smallest option, but a student cannot confirm it in one routine step - 9 is a difference, so checking it needs both ends 5 and 14 and the failures at 4 and 15. Bypass: skipping the attained-endpoint decision (treating ≥ -60 as > -60) gives exactly 11, above the key as the slot plans. Test-wise: a student who stops at the greatest qualifying k answers 14. Read lines: DPAIR 9 + 11 = 20 = 19 + 1 - 1 is not printed, and adding the key to a distractor is not a step of the problem; the 20 is the count at the failing ends k = 4 and 15, which a student uses but does not add to any option. D4 'greatest' - the ask is a difference (greatest minus least), not a greatest value. PROBE: the item goes to the cold probe as a try-1 aggregate; confirming 9 needs both ends 5 and 14. FAR, BOUND, STRUCT, INTER are answered in their own fields. IDEA: the part setup is the probed setup with one word changed (the second inequality); same idea, probed before writing.
